title: Deque
html:
A deque (double-ended queue, pronounced “deck”) lets you insert and delete at both ends in O(1). It is a stack and a queue in one container, and the workhorse behind sliding-window problems, undo histories and work-stealing schedulers.

Deque — a linear data structure that generalises the stack and the queue: elements can be added or removed at the front and at the rear, all in O(1). Access to the middle may or may not be supported depending on the implementation.

Operations

OperationWhat it doesTime
insertFront(x)Add x before the current frontO(1)
insertRear(x)Add x after the current rearO(1)
deleteFront()Remove and return the front elementO(1)
deleteRear()Remove and return the rear elementO(1)
getFront() / getRear()Peek at either endO(1)
isEmpty() / isFull()Empty check; isFull() only for fixed-capacity dequesO(1)
size()Number of elementsO(1)

The same operations have different names in every library — this table is worth memorising, because it is also the stack and queue API of each language:

Python collections.dequeC++ std::dequeJava ArrayDeque (Deque<T>)JavaScript Array
insertFrontappendleft(x)push_front(x)offerFirst(x) / addFirst(x) / push(x)unshift(x) — O(n)
insertRearappend(x)push_back(x)offerLast(x) / addLast(x) / offer(x)push(x)
deleteFrontpopleft()pop_front()pollFirst() / removeFirst() / pop() / poll()shift() — O(n)
deleteRearpop()pop_back()pollLast() / removeLast()pop()
getFront / getReard[0] / d[-1]front() / back()peekFirst() / peekLast()a[0] / a[a.length - 1]
Watch out

JavaScript has no built-in deque. unshift() and shift() re-index the whole array, so they are O(n). For small inputs that is fine; for sliding windows over large arrays, implement a deque yourself (circular array or doubly linked list — both below) or keep two indices into a plain array.

Where deques are used

Stack and queue in one

A deque does everything both do, so one implementation (Python's deque, Java's ArrayDeque) serves as the standard stack and the standard queue.

History of actions

Browser history, undo buffers, “recently used” lists: push new actions at one end, drop the oldest from the other when the history is full (deque(maxlen=n) does this automatically).

Work-stealing schedulers

Each worker thread keeps its tasks in a deque: it pushes and pops at the rear (LIFO, cache-warm); idle threads steal from the front (the oldest, largest tasks). Used by Java's ForkJoinPool and Go's runtime.

Two-level priority queue

Urgent items go to the front, normal items to the rear, always serve the front — a priority queue with exactly two priorities, as in 0-1 BFS on graphs with edge weights 0 and 1.

Sliding window maximum / minimum

Maximum of every subarray of size k in O(n): the deque keeps candidate indices in decreasing order of value — see DSA Advanced → Sliding Window.

Palindromes and symmetry checks

Compare the two ends and remove both until the middle is reached — solved below.

Using the built-in containers

Python's deque also has a handful of list-like extras. They are convenient, but note which of them walk the whole structure (next section).

Pitfall

extendleft([10, 20]) produces 20, 10, … — it calls appendleft for each element in turn, so the sequence appears reversed. Pass reversed(items) if you want to keep their order.

Time complexities and internal working

ComplexityPython deque operationsWhy
O(1)append, appendleft, pop, popleft, len, d[0], d[-1]both ends are directly reachable
O(n)d[i] in the middle, count(x), insert(i, x), remove(x), x in d, reverse()must walk the blocks from one end
O(min(k, n − k))rotate(k)moves k elements one by one, going the shorter way round
O(len(l))extend(l), extendleft(l)one append / appendleft per element

CPython's deque is a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks (64 slots each). The ends live in the leftmost and rightmost blocks, so pushing or popping at either end touches one slot and occasionally allocates or frees one block; walking to d[i] means hopping i // 64 blocks, hence O(n) in the middle.

LibraryInternal structureBoth endsRandom access d[i]
Python collections.dequedoubly linked list of 64-slot blocksO(1)O(n) in the middle, O(1) near the ends
C++ std::dequearray of pointers to fixed-size chunks (“map of blocks”)O(1)O(1) — two lookups
Java ArrayDequecircular, growable array (doubles when full)amortised O(1)not supported (no get(i))
Java LinkedListdoubly linked list of nodesO(1)O(n)
Key point

std::deque is the one standard deque with O(1) indexing, which is why std::stack and std::queue adapt it by default. Java's ArrayDeque is faster and leaner than LinkedList for stack/queue work (one array, no per-node objects) but refuses null elements.

Implementing a deque with a doubly linked list

A singly linked list gives O(1) at the head and, with a tail pointer, O(1) insertRear — but deleteRear needs the node before the tail, which only a walk from the head can find: O(n). A doubly linked list stores a prev pointer in every node, so tail = tail.prev is one step and every deque operation is O(1).

1
insertFront(x) / insertRear(x)
Create a node. If empty, head = tail = node. Otherwise link it before head (set node.next, head.prev, head) or after tail (set node.prev, tail.next, tail).
2
deleteFront() / deleteRear()
Advance head = head.next (or tail = tail.prev). If the deque became empty set the other pointer to null too; otherwise clear the new end's dangling prev (or next).
3
Both empty cases matter
The original notes did head = head.next; head.prev = None without checking — deleting the last element then crashes on None.prev. Guard it.
Example

Input: insertRear 10 20 30; deleteFront; deleteRear; insertFront 100, 1000
Output: front/rear: 10/30 → 20/30 → 20/20; final order 1000 100 20

Time O(1) per operationSpace O(n) for n elements

Implementing a deque with a circular array

The circular-array queue extends naturally: insertFront steps front backwards (wrapping from 0 to cap − 1), insertRear fills the slot after the rear (wrapping from cap − 1 to 0). Keeping front and size is enough — the rear index is always (front + size − 1) % cap, and size disambiguates empty from full.

Example

Input: capacity = 5; insertFront 10 20 30; insertRear 40 50; deleteFront; deleteRear
Output: order 30 20 10 40 50 → after deletes 20 10 40

Time O(1) per operationSpace O(cap)
Pitfall

Stepping the front backwards as front - 1 gives -1 when front == 0. In C++/Java that is an out-of-bounds read; in Python slots[-1] silently hits the last slot and leaves front negative. Always write (front - 1 + cap) % cap — and avoid the -1-means-empty sentinel of the original notes, which needs four special cases per operation; a size counter needs none.

Array or linked list?

The original notes list the array version's advantages as “random access, supports all operations, cache friendly, O(1) time”. Here is the full comparison:

Circular arrayDoubly linked list
Insert / delete at both endsO(1) (amortised O(1) if it grows by doubling)O(1)
Random access d[i]O(1) — slots[(front + i) % cap]O(n)
Memoryone contiguous block, no per-element overhead; some unused capacitytwo pointers per node, scattered allocations
Cache behaviourfriendly — neighbours are adjacent in memorypoor — every step is a pointer chase
Capacityfixed, or resize by doubling (copy O(n), rarely)unbounded, never copies
Used byJava ArrayDeque, C++ std::deque (chunked), Python deque (blocks)Java LinkedList
Do

Default to the array-based deque of your language: it is faster in practice and supports indexing. Reach for a linked list only when you need stable node references (an element must keep its identity while others are added) or truly unbounded growth without copying.

Problem: check whether a string is a palindrome

Example

Input: s = "Nurses run"
Output: Yes
Input: s = "hello"
Output: No

Idea

Load the cleaned characters into a deque, then repeatedly compare and remove the two ends. A palindrome reads the same from both directions, so every pair must match until at most one character is left.

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Pitfall

In Java, d.pollFirst() != d.pollLast() compares two Character objects by reference. It happens to work for ASCII because of the small-value cache, and silently fails beyond it — unbox to char (or use .equals) first. In JavaScript the array shift() makes this O(n²); two indices i, j walking inwards give the same answer in O(n) with no deque at all.

Key point

The flagship deque problem — maximum of every window of size k in O(n) — keeps the deque sorted by value with indices, popping from the rear anything smaller than the new element and from the front anything that has left the window. It is worked through in DSA Advanced → Sliding Window.

Interview Q&A

What is a deque, and how does it relate to stacks and queues?

A double-ended queue: insert and delete in O(1) at both the front and the rear. Use only one end and it is a stack; insert at the rear and delete at the front and it is a queue. That is why collections.deque and ArrayDeque are the recommended stack and queue in Python and Java.

Why does a deque need a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked one?

deleteRear() must make the previous node the new tail. In a singly linked list that node is only reachable by walking from the head — O(n). A prev pointer makes it tail = tail.prev, O(1). Everything else (head operations, tail insert) a singly linked list with a tail pointer can already do in O(1).

How does Python's deque give O(1) at both ends, and why is d[i] O(n)?

It is a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks (64 slots). The two ends live in the leftmost and rightmost blocks, so pushing or popping there touches one slot. Indexing the middle has to hop block by block from the nearer end — O(n/64), i.e. O(n). Use a list when you need random access, a deque when you need both ends.

ArrayDeque or LinkedList in Java?

ArrayDeque for stacks and queues: a circular growable array, cache-friendly, no per-element node objects, faster in practice. LinkedList only when you also need List operations (index-based insert/remove via an iterator) or must store null, which ArrayDeque rejects.

How do you implement a deque with a fixed array, and how do you tell empty from full?

Treat the array as a ring. insertFront moves front to (front − 1 + cap) % cap; insertRear writes at (front + size) % cap. Keep a size counter: empty when size == 0, full when size == cap. Without the counter front and rear coincide in both states and you have to waste one slot to disambiguate.

Name a problem where a deque beats both a stack and a queue.

Sliding window maximum: for each window of size k, the deque holds indices of candidates in decreasing value order. New elements evict smaller ones from the rear (they can never be a maximum again), and indices that fall out of the window are dropped from the front. Each index enters and leaves once — O(n) overall, versus O(nk) naively.
